what_it_does: Before a chip can be manufactured, engineers must verify that its logic blueprint (a textual description called RTL, or register-transfer level, that specifies every wire and gate) actually behaves correctly — a process called simulation. Simulating complex chips on ordinary CPUs is very slow, and dedicated hardware emulators (basically custom-built FPGAs — programmable chips that can be wired up to mimic another chip's logic) are fast but extremely expensive and hard to access. Graphics processors (GPUs) are cheap and massively parallel, but prior attempts to accelerate chip simulation on GPUs largely failed because circuits have wildly uneven, irregular structures that clash with the GPU's requirement that thousands of threads do the same thing at the same time. GEM solves this by borrowing an idea from FPGA emulators: it re-encodes the circuit as a 'virtual VLIW' (Very Long Instruction Word) program — a format where one wide instruction bundles many independent operations that can run in parallel — then maps that VLIW program onto CUDA (the programming model for NVIDIA GPUs) so the GPU's many cores all execute the same kind of instruction simultaneously, avoiding the divergence problem that crippled earlier approaches. The overall process mirrors how FPGA tools place and route a design onto hardware, but targets GPU cores instead.
